I imagine such a thing would work with a literal written social contract. Instead of the implied social contract we've all apparently consented to tacitly by existing, you'd explicitly agree to the terms of your participation within the community. You agree to do certain things and refrain from doing others and are in return rewarded with certain benefits of being a citizen.

The main differences between such a system and the one we currently have would be first that 'crimes' that don't actually go against the non-aggression principle (e.g. the non-aggression principle makes theft and murder inherently bad, but adhering to a dress code is a 'crime' you agreed not to commit) can't be punished in a method that itself goes against the NAP. So stealing might be punishable by imprisonment, but not paying your taxes would only be punishable by other means, like withholding benefits or expulsion from the community. Second you can basically leave whenever you want, so long as you don't owe anyone anything or haven't committed a crime. Don't like living under socialism? Just sign a few contracts and you might be able to change systems.

Obviously this is all speculation as nothing like this has ever existed ever.

While I find all of the comments and discussion interesting, I think a point should be made that any "pure" system is ultimately doomed to fail.

In my mind, without any cites or references:

Libertarianism: While small groups seem to work in the short run, eventually, someone goes too far and the community either attempts to expel the "extremist" (changing from "live and let live" to "no, you can't do that) OR the group is forced to impose limitations on who is suitable to be a member (let's close our borders and keep out those that won't fit in")

Socialism: At the outset, society can move in directions deemed best for all. However, over time the differences between individuals (don't even go there, that's not what I am talking about) will insure that some of us want to have more than others of some things (think "I want to be famous and get singular attention versus those of us that don't want all the attention") - this is why true socialism also tends to develop into "conformity is good" social setups.

Capitalism: Truly pure capitalism requires true competition, ease of entry to new competitors AND a populace that is educated enough to correctly pick the best products (think energy drinks - are any of them actually good for anybody?) Greed will win out whenever people aren't on their guard... Does anyone remember the Sherman Antitrust Act (this is still law, I think)? This law was used in past decades to "break up" certain monopolies that it was felt stifled competition. The breakup of the monopoly held by ATT back in the day was seen as a good thing. (The very idea of an organization that is too big to fail should be the definition of a monopoly.)

I digress...

Point is that in my mind society, because it's about people, needs to borrow from all different disciplines to be most effective. No one system is best.
